claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces cause premature failure in the untreated alloy.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 2 at.% Nb to the base eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The Nb-modified alloy is to be produced by conventional melting and homogenization.
A 2 at.% Nb addition will promote Nb segregation to lamellar-colony boundaries.
Segregated Nb will form a thin, ductile, Nb-enriched interfacial layer at lamellar boundaries.
Nb segregation lowers local lattice misfit and interface barrier strength.
The Nb-enriched interfacial layer enhances dislocation transmission across lamellar boundaries.
Enhanced slip transmission reduces the severity of dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Reduced dislocation pile-ups alleviate local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations delay or suppress microcrack nucleation during room-temperature deformation.
Minor Nb-rich precipitation may produce slight precipitation hardening.
The Nb addition is predicted to improve room-temperature fracture strain by approximately 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The Nb addition is predicted to maintain yield strength or increase it by approximately 5–10% relative to the untreated alloy.
The predicted benefit applies under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
The intervention requires controlled Nb segregation without formation of coarse, brittle Nb-rich secondary phases.
Coarse Nb-rich phases could cause embrittlement and negate the proposed benefit.
